title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a man swears off the slot machines, then hears the jingle from the next room. The Rig Veda keeps a gambler's own confession
tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: Ushas, the dawn, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come.

He promised. No more, not this time. He walks past the casino floor toward the exit, proud of himself. Then, from behind a row of machines, comes the bright little jingle of someone winning. His feet slow. The promise was real, and so is the pull, and the pull is winning. Anyone who has tried to quit a habit, a phone, a drink, may know that moment. One Rig Veda hymn is spoken by a gambler, in his own voice, and it doesn't hold back.
screen: `HE PROMISED. HE MEANT IT.` → `THEN THE SOUND OF WINNING.` → `A GAMBLER'S HYMN.`

segments.voice: He starts with the dice themselves. They thrill me, he says, in paraphrase, like a deep drink of soma. Then he tells what they cost. My wife never quarreled with me, never got angry. She was kind to me and to my friends. And for the sake of one losing throw, I drove away a devoted wife. Now his mother-in-law hates him, his wife pushes him away, and his own family says: we don't know him, take him away. Other men court his wife while the dice take his wealth. Then the line the hymn turns on. When I decide I won't play, he says, I fall behind as my friends go off. But when the brown dice are thrown and their sound reaches me, off I go to the meeting place like a lover to a lover. His resolve doesn't fail from lack of knowing better. It fails at the sound. Meanwhile his wife is left grieving, and his mother mourns a son wandering who knows where. Then a voice cuts through. Don't play with dice. Farm your field. Be glad of what you have, and value it. There are your cattle, there is your wife. So says Savitar, the god who rouses, linked with the sun. The hymn ends not at the gaming table but with a field, some cattle, and a wife at home.
screen: `THE DICE THRILL HIM LIKE SOMA.` · `HE DROVE AWAY A DEVOTED WIFE.` · `RESOLVE FAILS AT THE SOUND.` · `DON'T PLAY. FARM YOUR FIELD.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that gets past your good intentions, a phone, a snack, an old argument you keep picking up, and without scolding yourself, notice its trigger: a sound, a time of day, a feeling. Then picture your field, the plain good things in front of you, and rest there; if you pray, you can ask for strength in your own words.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns of fire, dawn and the one called by many names, and also a gambler's confession, ending with Savitar's advice: farm your field.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Even the gambler's hymn ends at home. Tomorrow, a hymn that asks how everything began.

screen: `DAY 1249 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NASADIYA SUKTA (THE HYMN OF CREATION — "WHO REALLY KNOWS?").`

howItsDone: The gambler's hymn is part of the Rig Veda's recited text, and Hindu teachers sometimes point to Savitar's advice in it, to leave the dice and tend one's field, as Vedic counsel against ruinous habits.

original.note: Sanskrit: a die, one of the dice. The gambler's hymn is sometimes called the akṣa sukta, the hymn of the dice.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Rig Veda is only about gods and rituals.
what it means: it also keeps a gambler's confession, in his own voice, about what the dice cost him.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.34, the dice hymn, where resolve breaks at the sound of the dice and Savitar's counsel closes it: farm your field, there are your cattle, there your wife.

chat.says: Is there really a hymn about gambling in the Rig Veda?
options: Yes, a gambler confesses what dice cost him, and Savitar says: farm your field.
Yes, a hymn that blesses the dice so the player will win more often.
No, gambling only shows up later, in stories like the Mahabharata.
chat.meaning: Rig Veda 10.34 is a gambler's own voice: his resolve fails at the sound of the dice, and Savitar tells him to farm his field.
